blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Every British meeting has two structures running at the same time. The visible one is on the agenda: welcome, item one, item two, any other business, next steps. The hidden one is the real architecture — who was consulted beforehand, who has already agreed, who is being deliberately given a chance to object for the record, and whose silence signals quiet assent to something they cannot support out loud.

What really happens in a senior British meeting is almost never captured by the minutes. The minutes tell you what was said; the hidden architecture tells you what was meant. A line like "the committee agreed to proceed, noting Mr Carter's reservations" can mean anything from full alignment to "everyone has quietly decided Mr Carter is wrong and the matter is closed".

Senior people read both structures at once. It is this dual reading that separates an executive from a manager: the willingness to see not only the room in front of you, but the conversations that led to the room, the conversations that will follow it, and the small, careful choreography by which British organisations make decisions appear to happen naturally.

items.q: According to the text, what does the visible structure of a meeting consist of?
options: The conversations held beforehand
The agenda items and running order
The choreography of the decision
The silences of those who disagree
items.why: "The visible one is on the agenda: welcome, item one, item two…" — é a pauta formal.

items.q: What do the minutes capture, according to the author?
options: What was meant
The quiet assent in the room
Who was consulted beforehand
What was said
items.why: "The minutes tell you what was said; the hidden architecture tells you what was meant."

items.q: The line "noting Mr Carter's reservations" is used to show that…
options: Mr Carter was formally overruled by a vote
the committee always records dissent in full
the same wording can conceal very different realities
reservations must be resolved before proceeding
items.why: "can mean anything from full alignment to 'everyone has quietly decided Mr Carter is wrong'" — a mesma frase esconde sentidos opostos.

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Decisions are often shaped before the meeting begins.
Silence in a meeting can carry real meaning.
The minutes are a reliable and complete record of what was decided.
Reading a meeting well requires attention to what is left unsaid.
items.why: Inferência: o texto argumenta que a ata quase nunca captura o que de fato aconteceu.

items.q: The phrase "make decisions appear to happen naturally" suggests that, in British organisations, decisions…
options: cannot be reached without open disagreement
are genuinely spontaneous and unplanned
are made only by the most senior person present
are actually engineered in advance but staged to look organic
items.why: Inferência: "appear to" indica encenação — a decisão é preparada nos bastidores e apresentada como natural.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Oliver orientando a nova vice-presidente. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let's take last week's strategy minutes and read them properly. On paper this is three tidy paragraphs. In reality, the whole thing was settled before anyone sat down.

Look at item two. "The committee agreed to proceed, noting Ms Whitfield's reservations." Now, what that actually tells you is that Whitfield lost, and she knows it. She was given her moment to object for the record — that is what "noting her reservations" is for — and then the room moved on. It is not a compromise; it is a polite burial.

And notice who says nothing at all. The finance director. His silence isn't neutrality. What his silence means is that he was consulted a fortnight ago, he agreed then, and he sees no reason to spend capital repeating himself in the room.

So here is what I'd have you do before the next one. Don't wait for the meeting to find out what has been decided. It is the corridor conversations, the quiet calls, the pre-reads, that carry the real weight. By the time we're in the room, the decision is usually just being ratified. Learn to read that, and you'll never be surprised by a set of minutes again.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What is Oliver's main point about last week's strategy meeting?
options: The committee failed to reach any conclusion
The real decision had been settled before the meeting began
Ms Whitfield's objection changed the outcome
The minutes were poorly written and inaccurate
items.why: "the whole thing was settled before anyone sat down."

items.q: How does Oliver interpret "noting Ms Whitfield's reservations"?
options: As a polite way of recording that she lost
As a genuine compromise between two positions
As a request for more information from her
As a sign the matter was postponed
items.why: "It is not a compromise; it is a polite burial."

items.q: What does Oliver say the finance director's silence means?
options: He was consulted earlier, agreed, and saw no need to repeat himself
He had not read the papers in advance
He disagreed but chose not to speak
He was neutral on the decision
items.why: "he was consulted a fortnight ago, he agreed then, and he sees no reason to spend capital repeating himself."

items.q: What does Oliver imply by "spend capital" in relation to the finance director?
options: That speaking up in meetings has a political cost worth conserving
That the meeting was about capital expenditure
That the director controls the department's budget
That the director was worried about the project's finances
items.why: Inferência: "spend capital" é metáfora — falar de novo gastaria influência/capital político sem necessidade.

items.q: What is Oliver's advice to the new vice-president?
options: To find out what has been decided before the meeting, through the informal conversations
To read the minutes more carefully after each meeting
To wait until the meeting to form her own view
To object for the record whenever she disagrees
items.why: Inferência: "Don't wait for the meeting… the corridor conversations… carry the real weight."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "He gave quiet assent with a single nod, and the item passed." Assent means…
options: a request for delay
formal abstention
open objection
agreement or approval
items.why: Assent = assentimento, concordância — muitas vezes tácita.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Two directors were quietly ___ over dinner long before the proposal ever reached the committee."
options: minuted
ratified
consulted
objected
items.why: Consulted = consultados de antemão — a conversa prévia do enredo da lição.

items.q: "The minutes recorded the outcome but not the manoeuvring behind it." The minutes are…
options: the list of attendees
the pre-meeting briefings
the timing of the meeting
the official written record of the meeting
items.why: Minutes = ata, o registro oficial do que foi dito e decidido.

items.q: "Her reservations were noted, and the committee moved on regardless." Reservations here means…
options: bookings made in advance
seats kept for senior members
doubts or objections about a decision
confidential documents
items.why: Reservations = ressalvas, reservas quanto a algo — não tem a ver com reserva de lugar.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "There was a careful ___ to the whole session: who spoke first, who deferred, who stayed silent — nothing was accidental."
options: assent
agenda
reservation
choreography
items.why: Choreography = coreografia — a orquestração cuidadosa dos gestos e falas, imagem central da lição.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem em reuniões de nível sênior. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The chair let each objector go on the record before closing the item." To go on the record means to…
options: leave the meeting early
have one's position formally noted
vote against the proposal
speak off the record, informally
items.why: Go on the record = ter a posição registrada formalmente — exatamente o "object for the record" da lição.

items.q: "By the time it reached the board, the decision was really just being rubber-stamped." This means it was…
options: debated at great length
sent back for revision
approved automatically, without genuine scrutiny
rejected on procedural grounds
items.why: Rubber-stamp = homologar sem questionar — a decisão já vinha pronta dos bastidores.

items.q: "Nobody said no outright, but you could feel the room closing ranks against her." To close ranks means to…
options: invite more people into the debate
openly criticise someone
unite in support of one another, often to exclude an outsider
postpone the discussion
items.why: Close ranks = cerrar fileiras, unir-se em bloco — muitas vezes para isolar quem discorda.

items.q: "Most of the real work had been done in advance, to square things away before the meeting." To square things away means to…
options: raise new problems
distribute the agenda
settle and finalise matters neatly
escalate a dispute
items.why: Square away = deixar tudo resolvido e alinhado de antemão.

items.q: "He never argued in the room; he preferred to have a quiet word beforehand." To have a quiet word means to…
options: speak privately and informally to influence someone
say nothing at all
raise the issue loudly in public
send a formal written memo
items.why: Have a quiet word = trocar uma palavra em particular — a conversa de corredor que decide antes da reunião.
